newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil re-election bill to sail through panel - poll.
newsitem.headline: Brazil re-election bill to sail through panel - poll.

text.p: A constitutional amendment that would give Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso the chance of a second term will sail through a lower house committee vote next week, the daily O Estado de Sao Paulo predicted on Wednesday.
A poll by the newspaper of the committee's 30 members found 19 deputies in favor of the amendment and 11 against.
The newspaper said Cardoso would be the most popular candidate in the 1998 presidential elections, if he were allowed to stand.

A survey by the private Brazilian Opinion Poll Institute said the president would win 38 percent of the vote followed by Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers Party's runner-up in the last two presidential elections, with 14 percent.
The survey heard the views of 2,000 voters across Brazil during December. The margin of error was not given.

Should Congress reject re-election and sideline Cardoso from the race, Jose Sarney, Brazilian president between 1985-89, and former Sao Paulo mayor Paulo Maluf would each win 18 percent of the vote, followed by Lula with 16 percent, Estado said.
The polls are a boost for the government as it enters a decisive phase in its drive to muster support for re-election.
Estado's prediction of an easy passage for the amendment in its lower house committee tallies with general expectations.

That vote is expected to take place on January 13, followed two days later by the first of two votes on the floor of the Chamber of Deputies. Government leaders say at least 320 deputies will vote in favor of re-election, more than the 308 votes needed for approval of constitutional amendments.
Opponents of re-election insisted the government was bluffing and did not have enough votes.

The Brazilian Progressive Party (PPB), of former Sao Paulo mayor and presidential hopeful Maluf, was due to meet later on Wednesday to mull a possible legal challenge to the calling of an extraordinary session of Congress to deal with re-election.

But the PPB's president, Senator Espiridiao Amin, who is a rival of Maluf, was quoted as saying half the party's deputies would vote in favor of re-election, making it impossible to prevent its approval.
